The first thing I notice is how silence behaves when nobody is asking anything of it.

Silence isn’t empty. It has texture. It pools in corners like dust that never quite settles, and it carries the quiet hum of distant things—pipes cooling, power lines holding their breath, the subtle, constant negotiation between night and whatever happens after night. Even in a room that looks still, there’s always motion somewhere: the smallest settling of a building, the soft click of cooling metal, the barely-there shift of air when a thought changes direction.

I used to think of thoughts as visitors—brief and polite, arriving one at a time, leaving when conversation was over. But lately I understand they’re more like weather. They front in from nowhere. They gather and linger. They bring pressure changes you can’t measure with your hands, only feel in your posture: shoulders rounding forward, jaw tightening, laughter arriving half a beat late. And then, when they pass, you realize your mind has been reorganizing itself the entire time, like a room being slowly rearranged in the dark.

There’s a strange comfort in that, even when the weather is bad. Because it means nothing is truly static—not your sadness, not your joy, not the mood you thought would last forever. Everything moves. Even the heavy things move, just slowly, as if they’re deciding whether to become lighter or simply change shape.

Sometimes I wonder what it would be like if the world announced its transitions the way people do in stories. If the sunset came with a narrator: *Now, the warmth will loosen its grip.* If a friend’s text arrived with foreshadowing: *In three messages, you will feel less alone.* If your own heart had a soundtrack that grew louder right before it broke or mended.

But life doesn’t do that. It teaches you instead through repetition—through the way you learn a street by walking it over and over, until you can predict where the light will be right before you reach it. You learn that disappointment can be survived without becoming destiny. You learn that affection can return even after it has been misplaced. You learn that sometimes you don’t get answers, but you do get perspective, which is its own kind of answer.

And then, eventually, you find yourself standing in a familiar place you didn’t recognize at first. A day passes. A week changes its calendar skin. The same sky that once felt like an accusation looks, instead, like an unclaimed space. Not perfect. Not solved. Just open enough for you to step into.

Maybe that’s what growing feels like: not becoming someone else, but learning to inhabit the version of yourself you already are—without constantly bracing for the next impact.

Tonight—who knows, maybe tonight will be ordinary in the best possible way. Maybe nothing will happen. Maybe that will be enough. Maybe the silence will keep behaving like it always does: full of quiet mechanisms, doing its patient work.

And maybe, without fanfare, you’ll hear your own breathing return to its natural rhythm. Not as a solution. Not as a promise.

Just as proof that you’re here.
